To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

embryonic stem cells with GLUT1-haplodeficiency are more susceptible to stress than wild type cells, and that this increased stress susceptibility can be explained by the partial GLUT1 compensational response.

embryonic stem cells are protected from glucose transporter protein type I (GLUT1-)haploinsufficiency by a partial compensatory response that is overwhelmed by inhibition of oxidative phosphorylations or hypoxia.
heterozygous knockout murine embryonal stem cells have reduced expression of GLUT1, impaired glucose metabolism in the absence of hypoxia and are more vulnerable to apoptosis under hypoxia.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of GLUT haploinsufficiency in the survival of embryonic stem cells in response to hypoxia and inhibition of oxidative phosphorylaiton.
the implications of glucose transporter protein GLUT1-haplodeficiency in embryonal stem cells for their glucose metabolism and survival in response of hypoxic stress.
the effects of glucose transporter protein 1 (GLT1) haploinsufficiency in embryonic cells.

The main takeaway from our work is that
haplodeficiency for the glucose transporter GLUT1 is not compatible with the survival of murine embryonic cells.

embryonic stem cells are sensitive to GLUT1 deficiency and that the compensatory response to GLUT1 haploinsufficiency is incomplete, which may be relevant in the setting of preimplantation genetic diagnosis.
